title: 1 Kings 7:1–12
context: Chapter 6 closed with the LORD’s house finished after seven years of work (6:38). Chapter 7 opens with Solomon’s own building program, which took thirteen years (7:1); 1 Kings 9:10 later speaks of twenty years for the two houses together. The royal complex includes the House of the Forest of Lebanon, the hall of pillars, the porch of the throne where the king judged, Solomon’s own residence, and a house for Pharaoh’s daughter (compare 3:1 and 9:24), all built of costly cut stone and cedar. The narrator gives measurements and materials but does not comment on Solomon’s motives, so readers who see an implied contrast between the seven years and the thirteen do so by inference, not from an explicit statement in the text. A cubit is about 18 inches or 46 centimeters. Both traditions read this unit as constructive description that displays the wealth and order of Solomon’s kingdom; neither builds a doctrinal disagreement on the floor plans.

verses.text: Solomon was building his own house thirteen years, and he finished all his house.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon spends thirteen years on his own house. Arminian readers note that the text simply records the fact, and they are cautious about reading a rebuke into the comparison with the seven years spent on the temple (6:38). The verse shows a king using real freedom and resources, for good or ill, as the later story will test.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that the narrator states the length without comment. Some see a quiet contrast with the temple’s seven years, but the text does not make that judgment explicit. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a factual transition, with any evaluation of Solomon left to the narrator’s later verdict (11:4).

verses.text: For he built the House of the Forest of Lebanon. Its length was one hundred cubits, its width fifty cubits, and its height thirty cubits, on four rows of cedar pillars, with cedar beams on the pillars.
verses.arminianNotes: The House of the Forest of Lebanon is named for its rows of cedar pillars. Arminian readers see here the prosperity God promised Solomon (3:13) being put to use. Its later use for gold shields and gold vessels (10:17, 21) shows a king entrusted with real wealth and real responsibility for how he uses it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same building as evidence of God’s generous provision to Solomon, as he promised (3:13). The size and the cedar display the peace and wealth of the kingdom. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an account of royal splendor received as a gift from God, not as a coded doctrinal message.

verses.text: It was covered with cedar above over the forty-five beams that were on the pillars, fifteen in a row.
verses.arminianNotes: The roof of cedar rests on forty-five beams, fifteen in a row. Arminian readers do not press the numbers for hidden meaning; they see careful human planning and craftsmanship that God permits and blesses. The detail reflects a builder concerned with order and durability, using gifts God has given.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also resist allegorizing the beams. They note that Scripture records ordinary craftsmanship with care, which honors human labor as part of God’s good creation order. Shared ground: both read the verse as plain construction detail, and both affirm that skilled work is a legitimate way to serve God and neighbor.

verses.text: There were beams in three rows, and window was facing window in three ranks.
verses.arminianNotes: The beams in three rows and windows facing one another describe a well-lit, well-ordered hall. Arminian readers note that the narrator lingers on design and symmetry, inviting appreciation for skilled human work. They see no theological dispute here, only an account of what was built and how carefully.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly treat the window arrangement as architectural description. Precise dimensions and patterns reflect the order and peace of Solomon’s reign, which God established (2:46). Shared ground: both traditions affirm the goodness of beauty and craftsmanship and decline to find doctrine in the window frames.

verses.text: All the doors and posts were made square with beams; and window was facing window in three ranks.
verses.arminianNotes: Doors and posts made square, with windows facing in three ranks, repeat the theme of order and symmetry. Arminian readers see a king and his workers exercising real skill and judgment. The repetition of “window was facing window in three ranks” emphasizes the completeness of the design rather than any hidden symbolism.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same repetition and read it as the narrator’s way of stressing the hall’s orderly completeness. They see the peace of Solomon’s reign providing room for such construction. Shared ground: both read the verse as description, and both see God’s blessing as the setting for ordered human work.

verses.text: He made the hall of pillars. Its length was fifty cubits and its width thirty cubits, with a porch before them, and pillars and a threshold before them.
verses.arminianNotes: The hall of pillars, fifty cubits by thirty with a porch in front, adds to the palace complex. Arminian readers note that the narrator records these structures without praise or blame. A king’s buildings can serve justice and the common good, and the measure of Solomon will be how he rules within them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the hall as part of the royal administration that God had placed in Solomon’s hands. The text attends to function and proportion rather than symbolism. Shared ground: both traditions treat the hall as historical description that frames Solomon’s rule, not as a basis for doctrinal dispute.

verses.text: He made the porch of the throne where he was to judge, even the porch of judgment; and it was covered with cedar from floor to floor.
verses.arminianNotes: The porch of the throne, where Solomon was to judge, connects the building to the wisdom God gave him for justice (3:9–12, 28). Arminian readers note that a gift of wisdom calls for faithful use; the throne room is a place where that gift is to be exercised responsibly before God and the people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the porch of judgment places justice at the center of royal life. They connect it with God’s gift of wisdom to Solomon (3:12) and with the ideal of a king who judges rightly under God. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as linking royal architecture with the call to administer justice.

verses.text: His house where he was to dwell, the other court within the porch, was of the same construction. He made also a house for Pharaoh’s daughter (whom Solomon had taken as wife), like this porch.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon builds a house for Pharaoh’s daughter, whom he had married in a political alliance (3:1). Arminian readers note that the narrator records this without comment here, but later names her among the foreign wives who turned his heart (11:1, 4). The detail quietly introduces a choice whose consequences will unfold over time.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also note the link to 3:1 and 11:1 and see the narrator laying groundwork for the later account of Solomon’s decline. The marriage is recorded, not commended. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as historical description that anticipates a later warning, while declining to read more judgment into it than the text states here.

verses.text: All these were of costly stones, even of stone cut according to measure, sawed with saws, inside and outside, even from the foundation to the coping, and so on the outside to the great court.
verses.arminianNotes: The buildings are made of costly stones, cut to measure and sawed, from foundation to coping. Arminian readers see thorough, high-quality work by many laborers (compare 5:13–18). The verse shows the scale of human effort Solomon could command, and it implicitly raises the question of how such power would be used.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same costly materials and see the fruit of the peace and wealth God granted to Solomon’s kingdom. Nothing is done cheaply or carelessly. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as describing excellent craftsmanship, while leaving to the wider narrative any assessment of the labor and resources involved.

verses.text: The foundation was of costly stones, even great stones, stones of ten cubits and stones of eight cubits.
verses.arminianNotes: The foundations are great stones of ten and eight cubits. Arminian readers note the emphasis on solid, lasting construction. They read the detail plainly as evidence of careful building and do not make it carry a theological point; the stability of the kingdom itself will depend on covenant faithfulness (6:12; 9:4–7).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly read the great foundation stones as a sign of permanence and strength in Solomon’s building work. Some draw a general lesson about building on a sure foundation, but the text itself offers no such comment. Shared ground: both traditions treat the verse as straightforward description of quality construction.

verses.text: Above were costly stones, even cut stone, according to measure, and cedar wood.
verses.arminianNotes: Above the foundations are costly cut stones and cedar wood. Arminian readers see continued attention to excellent materials, reflecting the means and skill available in Solomon’s day. The verse offers no moral comment, and they are content to receive it as part of an honest record of the king’s works.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise take the verse as a straightforward description of the upper construction. They note that the same materials, cut stone and cedar, appear in the temple, linking the two building projects. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as architectural detail without a separate doctrinal message.

verses.text: The great court around had three courses of cut stone with a course of cedar beams, like the inner court of the LORD’s house and the porch of the house.
verses.arminianNotes: The great court is built like the inner court of the LORD’s house, with three courses of cut stone and a course of cedar. Arminian readers note the deliberate likeness between palace and temple; the king’s house stands near the LORD’s house, and the king is called to rule as one accountable to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same likeness and see the king’s rule as meant to be ordered under the LORD’s rule, with palace and temple built in the same style and side by side. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as connecting the royal and the sacred while keeping the LORD’s house central to the narrative that follows.
